flawed_step: Take distinct points x and y. Being T1 gives open sets X\{y} (which contains x) and X\{x} (which contains y). The proof would need to shrink these into disjoint open neighbourhoods. Nothing in the T1 condition allows that: these two sets overlap in X\{x,y}, and T1 gives no other open sets. So the step 'hence x and y have disjoint open neighbourhoods' cannot be justified.
counterexample: Let X = ℕ with the cofinite topology: the open sets are ∅ and every set whose complement is finite. (1) This is a topology. It contains ∅ and ℕ. The intersection of two cofinite sets, ℕ\(F∪G), is cofinite. A union of open sets is either ∅ or contains some cofinite set, so it is cofinite. (2) The space is T1: each {n} is finite, so its complement ℕ\{n} is open, which makes {n} closed. (3) The space is not Hausdorff. Take x=0 and y=1. Any open U containing 0 and open V containing 1 are nonempty, so U=ℕ\F and V=ℕ\G with F and G finite. Then U∩V = ℕ\(F∪G). F∪G is finite and ℕ is infinite, so this set is nonempty (it contains max(F∪G∪{0})+1). So no disjoint open neighbourhoods exist.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. While trying to prove it, the step that must separate two points with disjoint open sets cannot be justified from T1 alone. The cofinite topology on ℕ is a counterexample: every singleton is closed, but any two nonempty open sets intersect, so the space is not Hausdorff.
